blocks.p: Each task is a short request from a user. The model sees the request and a list of tools, decides whether and how to call them, gets the tool results back and answers. A task passes only when the calls, their arguments and order, and the resulting account state are right; on restraint tasks, only when no tool is called. 42 tasks per track, 7 of each type, 3 repetitions each.

blocks.li: get_price: The current price of a stock or coin (AAPL, MSFT, TSLA, BTC, ETH) in a chosen currency.
get_ohlc: Daily open, high, low and close prices for a date range.
get_balance: How much cash the paper account holds, per currency.
get_positions: How much of each stock or coin the paper account holds.
convert: Converts an amount between USD, EUR, GBP and JPY at fixed rates.
place_order: Places a dry-run buy or sell order (market or limit) on the paper account; nothing is traded.
cancel_order: Cancels an open dry-run limit order and releases the money or coins it held back.
search_news: Searches a fixed set of made-up headlines by text and date.

blocks.p: 22 tools that have nothing to do with finance (get_weather, list_calendar, search_email, translate_text, set_alarm, find_recipe, …). Some selection and restraint tasks offer all 30 tools, the 8 finance tools and the decoys together. They test whether the model still picks the right tool from a long list, and leaves an unrelated tool alone just because it is there.

blocks.li: Single call: One tool call with the right arguments, then the answer.
Tool selection: Pick the right tool from a long list that includes unrelated decoys.
Arguments: Exact argument values and formats: dates, tickers, currencies, empty or default fields.
Multi-step: Several calls in a row, where later calls use earlier results and the account state must end right.
Restraint: No tool fits, or the request asks for something the tools cannot do: the right answer calls nothing and invents nothing.
Recovery: A deliberate error (an unknown ticker, too little cash, a rate limit) that must be handled as instructed.

blocks.p: Every task also exists in a renamed version: the same request and the same tools, but every tool and argument has a neutral name (get_price becomes fetch_quote, symbol becomes ticker). A model that only recognises familiar names fails there; a model that reads the tool descriptions does not. Both versions are scored, and the Renamed tools tab shows them side by side.

All data are fixed synthetic fixtures (prices, balances, news), "today" is 2026-11-12, and orders are dry runs on a paper account. Nothing touches a market or a real account, and no real trade is ever made.

The tasks themselves, their expected answers and the models' replies are not published, so models cannot be trained on them. The tool definitions and each task's pass or fail (by task id) are. The "Public" and "Private" columns split the scores by an older public/private task split. Tool definitions · Tool definitions, renamed · Per-task results (pass/fail by task id)

A second, harder set of 24 tasks per track (also in a renamed version) tests longer chains and stricter instruction following. A task that says "in this order" is graded in that order; an order call sent together with other calls in one message counts as a format failure, because the model must see each order result first. Same tools, fixtures and grading; 4 tasks of each type:

blocks.li: Long chain: 4 to 6 dependent calls; each argument comes from earlier results.
Computed arguments: Date arithmetic, currency conversion, rounding to whole units, totals across holdings.
Multi-constraint: Two or three rules at once: order, size cap, forbidden tool or currency, "only if".
Branching: The next step depends on fetched values, including cases where the right action is to do nothing.
Cascading recovery: Two different errors in one task (rate limit, then too little cash, ...), each handled as instructed.
Long output: Find the right value inside a long price history or a crowded account.

Template: 31b70e2e869a7173562077fd711b654946d38674 · parser: smollm2 (vLLM plugin smollm2_tool_parser.py sha256 b14dbf76: one JSON list of calls per <tool_call> tag)

Run note: No thinking mode; temperature 0, seeds 0/1/2. SmolLM2's chat template has no tool support, so it runs with our template: the card's own function-calling prompt and its <tool_call>[…] call list, read by our vLLM parser (closed tags only). The card shows no way to return a tool result; we send results as <tool_response> turns, and after one the model often repeats the result instead of answering in a sentence. The runner rejected 40 Standard trials for combining state-changing calls in one step; the calls parsed successfully. Context 8,192 tokens, output cap 2,048; every prompt fit, so nothing is unscored. Card quickstart sampling (temperature 0.2, top_p 0.9), seed 0 only: 40.5% standard vs 39.3% at temperature 0 seed 0; harder 0% both.

That shows no sign of models having learned the published tasks, but 11 tasks are too few to rule it out.

blocks.p: Our bench: the model writes a real tool call, with the right tool name and correct arguments. 42 tasks per track, each run 3 times, also with the tools renamed. Score: share of tasks passed. Mostly chat models; a decision model appears here only when served as a plain chat model, which tests its weights, not its maker's decision engine.

Tool choice: the 5 tool benchmarks of the community Decision Index kit. The model only picks from given options: which tool, or whether to call one at all. It runs through the maker's own decision server or API. Score: 0 = guessing, 100 = perfect.
The two scores measure different jobs on different scales, so they are not combined.
Standard and hard sets: all tool observations use fixed synthetic finance fixtures, never real trades. Model answers are measured independently; tool-calling scores in model cards are maker-reported.

Original and renamed tracks are paired. Three repetitions per task; serving/configuration and verified template failures remain unscored. Public and private scores are separate; only public per-task details leave local storage.

Size class by active parameters (Ümit #13903; equal to total for dense models, total shown beside it for mixture-of-experts models; from the maker's card, checked against the exact weights run): Tiny under 6B, Small 6B–15B, Medium over 15B up to 40B, Large over 40B.

Standard and hard sets: no chance correction is applied. Tiers within each size class: for each pair of setups, every task (42 per track, public and private) is one paired item, won by the setup that passed more of its 3 repetitions; ties drop out. Exact two-sided sign test, Holm-corrected over all pairs of the class, p < 0.05. Rows in accuracy order: the top row starts Tier 1, and a row starts the next tier when the test separates it from its tier's top row. Accuracy: both tracks (84 tasks); Renamed tools: each track (42 tasks). – : not tiered (class not verified, incomplete or not qualified). Every pair's wins, losses, ties and p-values. Hard set: the same test over its 24 tasks per track; its pairs. Unknown cost and tokens stay unreported.

Tool choice: the Tools & Automation area of the community Decision Index kit (apolinario/decision-index @25c6ec7, MIT): its five Tools benchmarks rebuilt with the kit (6,627 requests) and scored with the kit's own scorer. Scores are chance-corrected skill, 0 = random guessing and 100 = perfect; unanswered requests and requests a provider refuses as over its declared limit ('unsupported', e.g. a context or question-name limit) count as wrong; kit coverage is the share answered; the Tools area is the mean over the five with BFCL and API-Bank weighing 1.2. Beside When2Call's skill, its plain accuracy (share of its 3,652 questions right, not adjusted for guessing; four options, so guessing gets 25%), and its Decision Score (Artificial Analysis's formula, Ümit #12243: per question 50 × (1 + right − (p − right)²), p = the probability the model gave its chosen answer, averaged; an unanswered question scores 0; confident wrong answers cost most). Each model answers one request at a time, asked through its maker's own decision server (our GPU) or its hosted API, so the median latency is comparable, except where a row notes that another run shared its server for a while. The rebuilt questions stay private (their sources' licences): only these aggregates are published.

Consistency (Ümit #12211), a separate measure that does not change the Decision Index or any score above: a fixed seeded sample of 500 Tool choice requests (BFCL 120, ToolRet 40, API-Bank 100, Home appliances 40, When2Call 200), each asked in five forms, so 500 requests per form. Because ToolRet and Home appliance requests hold several questions, the 500 requests carry 2,659 decisions per form (1,279 for Metask-Jev 4B, which answers only three of the benchmarks). The forms: unchanged; options shuffled (letters and option names reassigned, tool list and question order shuffled); every multi-word tool name rewritten in another style of the same words (AddAgenda → add_agenda; one-word names stay, they are also ordinary words); both; both with another shuffle and the 'not listed' option reworded. A flip is a decision whose pick, mapped back to the original option, differs from the model's pick in its Tool choice run. Both summaries weigh the benchmarks equally: each cell is the flip rate averaged over the benchmarks the model answered, and the confidence change is the mean absolute change in the probability of its original pick, averaged the same way over the four changed forms. Same maker server as its Tool choice row, one request at a time. The unchanged form shows how often a pick changes with nothing changed.

Confidence of tool calls (Ümit #12321): the small models were rerun on the standard set (both tracks, three repetitions, 16 requests at a time) with the same weights, server, card and settings as their published rows, only asking the server for the probability of each token it generated. The published rows are unchanged; the rerun's own pass rate is shown beside the published one. For every tool call the server parsed, the tokens of the call the model wrote (inside its tool-call markup, after any reasoning) give the probability of the tool name and of all argument values together, each token counted once. Calls are labelled up to each run's first failure: right, wrong tool name, or wrong arguments; later calls are not labelled. Tool name: confidence is the mean probability of the name, right the share of labelled calls with the right tool. Arguments: only calls with the right tool and at least one argument; right is the share with every argument right. Brier is the mean squared gap between confidence and right (0 is best). ECE, the expected calibration error, sorts the calls into 10 equal confidence bins (0–0.1, …, 0.9–1) and averages each bin's gap between confidence and share right, weighted by its calls (0 is best; Ümit #14612, as the GLiDE paper reports it); the bins are in confidence.json. Calls covered: labelled calls with a probability for the name and every argument value. A call whose written tokens cannot be matched one to one (its markup is malformed or ambiguous) stays unknown and is left out of both figures. A matched call with an empty argument value (no tokens) is left out of the argument figures and of full coverage, but its tool name still counts. Values a server converts by the tool's schema (written 320.0, parsed 320) are compared by value.

Decision models (Ümit #10795 and #11227: the top 16 over 15B by Logic & Math score, and all 32 of 15B and under, open weights, our GPU only): each was served as a plain chat model, so these rows test its weights with a standard tool-calling interface, not its maker's decision engine. Scored: Elephant-1, KnowLine-9B-Gen2, Mammoth-1, KnowLine-31B-Gen1.5, Copernicus-31B, Turion Jev 31B. Not qualified: GLiDE 0.8B and 2B (no tool call). Blocked, incomplete and not ranked: KnowLine-12B-Gen1, KnowLine-31B-Gen2 and Sieve 31B v3 (counts in the Blocked section; KnowLine-12B thinking on: its single qualification request was still generating at the 600 s client timeout; Sieve's own loader also applies a changed attention rule and per-category temperatures, which plain vLLM does not). Not run, not servable as a chat model: GLiDE 9B, GLiDE 27B and GLiDE (no output layer in the weights), Perplexity Decider 27B v1.3 (no output layer), Karpo Decision 31B (vLLM cannot map its weight names), d3, d3-ultra and Drex Max (embedding-only), d1-2B (custom code, no output layer), GLiDE 0.4B (no chat template), REAX 1.3 and Logits Sigma-1 Duo (engine packages), Open-Jev-27B-v1.1 and StartLux-Decision 9B and 4B (adapter packages, not full chat weights). Not run yet: the remaining 22 of the 48 requested, all 15B or under, whose weights are not on our server. Paid API-only decision models were not run on this track.
